summary: Around 3100 BCE the farming chiefdoms along the Nile were united into a single kingdom, traditionally by Narmer. The river's yearly flood fed a dense population ruled by a god-king, the pharaoh, through scribes, priests and provincial governors. Historians divide its long history into the Old Kingdom, when the great pyramids were built, the Middle Kingdom, and the New Kingdom, when warrior pharaohs built an empire stretching from Nubia into Syria. Periods of division and foreign rule, by Libyans, Kushites, Assyrians and Persians, alternated with revivals. After Alexander the Great's conquest in 332 BCE Egypt was ruled by the Greek Ptolemies, and its independence ended when Cleopatra VII died and Rome annexed the country in 30 BCE.
legacy: Egypt gave the world monumental stone architecture, one of the first writing systems and a 365-day calendar, and its pyramids and mummies still fascinate people everywhere.

summary: Sumer, in the marshy south of Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), was home to the world's first cities. Between about 3500 and 3000 BCE towns such as Uruk grew into cities of tens of thousands, organised around temples that managed irrigation, grain and trade. To keep records, Sumerian scribes invented cuneiform writing on clay tablets around 3200 BCE. Sumer was never one country: a dozen rival city-states, each with its own patron god and king, fought over water and fields. Sargon of Akkad conquered them around 2334 BCE, but after Akkad's fall the Third Dynasty of Ur reunited the region and built a centralised state with a vast bureaucracy. Ur fell to Elamite invaders in 2004 BCE, and Sumerian gradually died out as a spoken language.
legacy: Sumer pioneered writing, early wheeled vehicles, the base-sixty counting behind our hours and minutes, and the first stories of Gilgamesh.

summary: Often called the world's first empire, Akkad was founded by Sargon, a man of humble origins who rose to serve the king of Kish and then seized power around 2334 BCE. Sargon conquered the quarrelling Sumerian city-states and campaigned as far as Syria and western Iran, uniting speakers of Sumerian and the Semitic Akkadian language under one ruler. He installed loyal governors, standardised weights and measures, and made Akkadian a language of administration. His grandson Naram-Sin pushed the borders further and was the first Mesopotamian king to call himself a god. Revolts, pressure from the Gutian mountain peoples and possibly a severe drought broke the empire apart, and by about 2154 BCE it had collapsed.
legacy: Akkad set the model of a multi-ethnic empire run from one capital, and Akkadian became the diplomatic language of the Near East for over a thousand years.

summary: Babylon was a small town until an Amorite dynasty made it a capital around 1894 BCE. Its sixth king, Hammurabi, conquered all of southern Mesopotamia and is remembered for his law code carved on a stone pillar. Over the next thousand years Babylon was ruled by Kassites, native kings and, for long stretches, the Assyrians, yet it remained the region's religious and cultural heart, famous for its scholars and astronomers. In 626 BCE Nabopolassar, traditionally called a Chaldean, threw off Assyrian rule and, allied with the Medes, destroyed Assyria. His son Nebuchadnezzar II built a Neo-Babylonian empire, rebuilt Babylon with the Ishtar Gate and captured Jerusalem in 587 BCE. Cyrus the Great of Persia took the city without a fight in 539 BCE.
legacy: Babylonian law, mathematics and astronomy, including the division of the circle into 360 degrees, shaped later Persian, Greek and Jewish thought.

summary: Assyria grew from the trading city of Assur on the upper Tigris, whose merchants ran caravans into Anatolia soon after 2000 BCE. After centuries as a regional kingdom it became a great power, and from the 9th century BCE its kings built the largest empire the world had yet seen. The Neo-Assyrian state had a professional standing army, iron weapons, siege engines and a road and messenger system, and it ruled through provinces under appointed governors. Rebellious peoples were deported en masse to break resistance. At its height Assyria controlled Mesopotamia, the Levant and, briefly, Egypt. Civil war after Ashurbanipal weakened it, and a coalition of Babylonians and Medes sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE; the last Assyrian army was defeated in 609 BCE.
legacy: Assyria invented much of the machinery of imperial rule later copied by Persia, and Ashurbanipal's library preserved thousands of cuneiform texts, including the Epic of Gilgamesh.

summary: The Hittites, speakers of the oldest recorded Indo-European language, built a kingdom in central Anatolia (modern Turkey) around 1650 BCE with its capital at Hattusa. An early king, Mursili I, raided as far as Babylon and sacked it in 1595 BCE. After a period of weakness, Suppiluliuma I made the Hittites a great power in the 14th century BCE, defeating the Mitanni and taking control of Syria, where he set up his sons as vassal kings. The Hittites were famed for their chariots and diplomacy, and after the Battle of Kadesh against Egypt they signed one of the earliest known peace treaties. Around 1180 BCE, amid the wider Bronze Age collapse, Hattusa was abandoned and the empire broke into small Syro-Hittite kingdoms.
legacy: The Hittite-Egyptian treaty is a landmark of international diplomacy, and the Hittite archives revealed a lost civilisation known before only from brief mentions in the Bible and in Egyptian records.

summary: The Indus or Harappan civilisation flourished along the Indus river and its neighbours in what is now Pakistan and north-west India. Farming villages grew into planned cities after about 2600 BCE, the Mature Harappan phase. Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were laid out on grids, with baked-brick houses, covered drains, possible granaries and, at Mohenjo-daro, a Great Bath, and standard weights and seals were used across an area larger than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined. Indus merchants traded with Mesopotamia by sea. Strikingly, no palaces, royal tombs or images of kings have been found, and the Indus script remains undeciphered, so we do not know how the cities were governed. After about 1900 BCE the cities were gradually abandoned, probably because of climate change and shifting rivers, and people dispersed into smaller villages.
legacy: The Indus cities set early standards in urban planning and sanitation, and many scholars trace continuities between Harappan crafts and later South Asian culture.

summary: The Minoans, named by the archaeologist Arthur Evans after the legendary King Minos, created Europe's first advanced civilisation on the island of Crete. From about 1900 BCE they built large palace complexes at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros, which acted as centres for religion, storage and craft production. Minoan ships traded across the eastern Mediterranean with Egypt and the Levant, and their colourful frescoes show bull-leaping, processions and sea life. They wrote in a script called Linear A, which is still undeciphered, so their rulers' names and language are unknown. After widespread destruction around 1450 BCE, possibly linked to earthquakes and the aftermath of the Thera eruption, Crete came under Mycenaean Greek control, and Minoan culture faded by about 1100 BCE.
legacy: Minoan art, architecture and seafaring strongly influenced Mycenaean Greece and inspired the Greek myths of the Minotaur and the labyrinth.

summary: After the collapse of the Mycenaean palaces, Greek communities slowly revived, and by about 800 BCE hundreds of independent city-states, or poleis, had emerged. Each polis was a city with its surrounding farmland, governed by kings, aristocrats, tyrants or citizen assemblies. Greeks founded colonies around the Mediterranean and Black Sea, from Marseille to Crimea. Athens developed the first democracy, while Sparta became a militarised state. Briefly united, the Greeks defeated the invading Persians at Marathon, Salamis and Plataea between 490 and 479 BCE. Rivalry between Athens and Sparta then led to the long Peloponnesian War. Weakened by constant conflict, the city-states fell under Macedonian domination after 338 BCE, and Rome took control of mainland Greece in 146 BCE.
legacy: Greek philosophy, democracy, drama, history writing, mathematics and the Olympic Games lie at the foundations of Western civilisation.

summary: Macedon was a kingdom in northern Greece that emerged in the 7th century BCE (later legend dated its founding to about 808 BCE); it was seen by many southern Greeks as half-barbarian. Philip II transformed it after 359 BCE, creating a professional army built around the long-speared phalanx and heavy cavalry, and in 338 BCE he defeated Athens and Thebes, making Macedon master of Greece. His son Alexander the Great invaded the Persian Empire in 334 BCE, won at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, took Egypt, Babylon and Persepolis, and marched to the Indus. When he died in Babylon in 323 BCE, aged 32, he left no adult heir; his generals fought over the empire and carved it into rival kingdoms. Macedon itself, ruled from 277 BCE by the Antigonids, was conquered by Rome after the Battle of Pydna in 168 BCE.
legacy: Alexander's conquests spread Greek language and culture from Egypt to Afghanistan, opening the Hellenistic age.

summary: The Seleucid Empire was the largest of the kingdoms formed from Alexander's conquests. Seleucus, one of Alexander's officers, seized Babylon in 312 BCE, the date from which the dynasty counted its years, and won most of the Asian provinces at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE. The Seleucids ruled a vast mix of peoples through Greek-style cities, governors and a Macedonian army, founding new towns such as Antioch. The empire was too large to hold: India was ceded to Chandragupta Maurya, Bactria broke away, and the Parthians took Iran. Antiochus III briefly restored its power but was defeated by Rome in 190 BCE. Later kings lost Mesopotamia to Parthia and quarrelled among themselves until Pompey annexed the remnant in Syria for Rome in 64 BCE.
legacy: The Seleucids spread Greek cities and culture across western Asia, and their attempt to Hellenise Judea provoked the Maccabean revolt remembered at Hanukkah.

summary: When Alexander's empire broke up, his general Ptolemy took Egypt, declared himself king in 305 BCE and founded the last dynasty of pharaohs. The Ptolemies were Macedonian Greeks who ruled from Alexandria, a new Greek city on the coast, while presenting themselves to Egyptians as traditional pharaohs and building temples to Egyptian gods. Egypt's grain made them rich, and they fought repeated wars with the Seleucids over Syria. Alexandria became the intellectual capital of the Greek world, with its Great Library, Museum and Lighthouse. From the 2nd century BCE dynastic feuds and revolts weakened the kingdom, which survived increasingly as a Roman client. Cleopatra VII allied with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, but after Antony's defeat at Actium she took her own life and Rome annexed Egypt in 30 BCE.
legacy: Ptolemaic Alexandria preserved and advanced Greek science and scholarship, and the Rosetta Stone, a Ptolemaic decree, later unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs.

summary: Carthage was founded on the coast of modern Tunisia by Phoenician settlers from Tyre, traditionally in 814 BCE. It grew into the leading Phoenician city in the west, building a commercial empire of trading posts and colonies across North Africa, southern Spain, Sardinia and western Sicily. Carthage was a republic run by wealthy merchant families, with two elected chief magistrates called suffetes and a council of elders, and it relied on a powerful navy and mercenary armies. Rivalry with Rome led to three Punic Wars. Carthage lost Sicily in the first, and in the second Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants and crushed Roman armies, but he was finally defeated at Zama in 202 BCE. In 146 BCE Rome besieged and destroyed the city.
legacy: Carthage spread Phoenician seafaring and the alphabet across the western Mediterranean, and Hannibal remains one of history's most studied generals.

summary: Nubia, the land along the Nile south of Egypt, was home to Africa's earliest kingdom outside Egypt. The Kerma culture built a powerful state from about 2500 BCE, which Egypt's New Kingdom conquered around 1500 BCE. As Egyptian control waned, a new Kushite kingdom arose at Napata, and in the 8th century BCE its kings Piye and Shabaka conquered Egypt, ruling it as the 25th Dynasty until the Assyrians drove them out around 664 BCE. The capital later moved south to Meroë, a centre of iron-smelting and trade in gold, ivory and ebony between Africa and the Mediterranean. Kushite rulers, including powerful queens called kandakes, built more pyramids than Egypt. Meroë declined in the 4th century CE and seems to have already collapsed when Aksum's armies raided the region around 350.
legacy: Kush shows that a great African civilisation flourished alongside Egypt, and its Meroitic script, still only partly understood, is one of Africa's oldest writing systems.

summary: Aksum rose in the highlands of what are now Eritrea and northern Ethiopia in the 1st century CE, growing rich from Red Sea trade through its port of Adulis, which linked the Roman world with Arabia and India. Aksumite kings controlled trade in ivory, gold and incense, minted their own gold, silver and bronze coins, and raised giant carved stone stelae over royal tombs. Around 340 King Ezana converted to Christianity, making Aksum one of the first Christian states. In the 6th century King Kaleb sent armies across the Red Sea to rule Yemen. The rise of Islam, and Persian and then Arab control of the sea routes, cut Aksum's trade, and by the 10th century the kingdom had faded as power shifted south.
legacy: Aksum founded the Ethiopian Orthodox Church and the Ge'ez script still used in Ethiopia and Eritrea, and its towering stelae remain national symbols.

summary: The Ghana Empire, known to its Soninke people as Wagadu, grew up in the Sahel between the Senegal and Niger rivers, in today's southern Mauritania and western Mali; it lay far from modern Ghana. From perhaps the 4th century its kings controlled the trade of West African gold northward across the Sahara in exchange for salt, copper and cloth, carried by camel caravans, and Arab writers called it the land of gold. The king ruled through tributary chiefs and taxed every load of goods crossing his realm. In the 11th century the Almoravid movement from the Sahara put pressure on Ghana and spread Islam. Weakened by drought, shifting trade routes and rebellious vassals, Ghana was overrun by the Sosso and then absorbed into Mali in the 13th century.
legacy: Ghana was the first of the great West African trading empires, and modern Ghana took its name in 1957 to honour it.

summary: The Mali Empire was founded by Sundiata Keita, the hero of a famous oral epic, who defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru at the Battle of Kirina around 1235. Mali's Mandinka rulers, called mansas, absorbed the old Ghana lands and expanded to control the gold fields of Bambuk and Bure and the trading cities of the Niger bend. Provinces and allied kingdoms paid tribute, and Islam spread among the ruling classes and merchants. Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, during which he gave away so much gold that he lowered its value in Cairo, made Mali famous as far as Europe, and Timbuktu became a centre of Islamic learning. From the 15th century succession disputes, Tuareg raids and the rise of Songhai stripped away its provinces, leaving a small Mandinka kingdom by the 17th century.
legacy: Mali made Timbuktu a legendary city of scholarship and trade, and the Epic of Sundiata is still performed by West African griots.

summary: Kanem arose around the 8th century among nomadic and farming peoples north-east of Lake Chad, at the southern end of a trans-Saharan trade route to Libya. Its kings of the Sayfawa dynasty, who reigned for about a thousand years, adopted Islam in the late 11th century and grew rich trading horses, salt and slaves. In the 13th century Dunama Dabbalemi expanded Kanem far into the Sahara. Civil wars and attacks by the Bulala people in the 14th century forced the dynasty to move west of Lake Chad to Bornu, where a new capital, Ngazargamu, was founded. Bornu reached its height under Idris Alooma in the late 16th century, using firearms and Turkish musketeers. It survived into the 19th century until the warlord Rabih az-Zubayr conquered it in 1893.
legacy: Kanem-Bornu was one of the longest-lasting states in world history and a major channel for Islam and Saharan trade in central Africa.

summary: Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a Shona-speaking kingdom on the southern African plateau, in the country now named after it. It grew after the earlier state of Mapungubwe in the 13th century, prospering by controlling gold mined on the plateau and large cattle herds, and trading through Swahili ports such as Sofala and Kilwa, which brought glass beads, Persian pottery and Chinese porcelain. Its rulers built immense dry-stone walls without mortar, including the Great Enclosure, with walls up to 11 metres high; at its height the city may have housed up to 10,000 people, though older estimates reach 18,000. In the 15th century the site was largely abandoned, perhaps because of overgrazing, exhausted resources and a shift of the gold trade northward, where the Mutapa and Torwa states took over.
legacy: Great Zimbabwe is the largest ancient stone complex in southern Africa; it disproved colonial claims that Africans could not have built it, and the modern nation took its name.

summary: Kongo was founded around 1390, traditionally by Lukeni lua Nimi, who conquered lands south of the lower Congo river in what is now northern Angola and western Congo. The king, or manikongo, ruled from Mbanza Kongo through appointed provincial governors, collected tribute in cloth and the shell money called nzimbu, and controlled a well-organised state. In 1483 Portuguese ships arrived, and King Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptised in 1491. His son Afonso I made Christianity the state religion and corresponded with the Portuguese and papal courts, but the growing Atlantic slave trade destabilised the kingdom. After defeat by the Portuguese at Mbwila in 1665, Kongo fell into decades of civil war. It survived as a weakened kingdom until Portugal absorbed it into colonial Angola, ending its last autonomy in 1914.
legacy: Kongo was a major Christian African kingdom, and its people and culture, carried across the Atlantic by the slave trade, deeply shaped the Afro-Caribbean and African American world.

summary: In 1270 Yekuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe dynasty and founded the Solomonic dynasty, claiming descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, a story later told in the Kebra Nagast. Its Christian emperors ruled the Ethiopian highlands from moving royal camps, and Amda Seyon and Zara Yaqob expanded the realm and strengthened the Orthodox Church. In the 16th century the Adal sultanate under Ahmad Gragn nearly destroyed the empire until Portuguese help arrived. Gondar became a fixed capital in the 1630s, but from 1769 the emperors lost power to regional lords. Tewodros II and Yohannes IV reunited the country, and Menelik II expanded it south and defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896. Apart from Italian occupation in 1936 to 1941, it stayed independent until Haile Selassie was overthrown in 1974.
legacy: Ethiopia was the only African state to defeat a European colonial army and keep its independence through the Scramble for Africa, making it a symbol of African freedom.

summary: The Fatimids were an Ismaili Shia dynasty claiming descent from the Prophet's daughter Fatima. Supported by Kutama Berber tribesmen, Abdallah al-Mahdi proclaimed himself caliph in Tunisia in 909, challenging the Sunni Abbasids of Baghdad. In 969 his descendant al-Mu'izz conquered Egypt, where his general founded Cairo, which became the new capital. At their height the Fatimids ruled North Africa, Egypt, Sicily, Syria, Palestine and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, growing rich from Red Sea and Mediterranean trade. They founded al-Azhar, one of the world's oldest universities. From the late 11th century the dynasty was weakened by military rivalries, famine, the loss of North Africa and Syria, and the Crusades. Saladin, their vizier, abolished the caliphate in 1171.
legacy: Fatimid Cairo, with al-Azhar and its great mosques and gates, became one of the leading cities of the Islamic world.

summary: The Almohad movement began with Ibn Tumart, a Berber religious reformer from the Atlas Mountains who in 1121 proclaimed himself the Mahdi and preached a strict doctrine of God's absolute oneness. His successor Abd al-Mu'min took the title of caliph, overthrew the Almoravids, captured Marrakesh in 1147 and went on to unite all of North Africa from Morocco to Tripoli, as well as Muslim Spain. The Almohads were great builders, raising the Koutoubia mosque in Marrakesh and the Giralda in Seville, and their court patronised philosophers such as Averroes. Their crushing defeat by the Christian Spanish kingdoms at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 began a rapid decline; provinces broke away to the Hafsids, Zayyanids and Marinids, who took Marrakesh in 1269.
legacy: The Almohads produced some of the finest Moorish architecture and fostered the philosophy of Averroes, which later shaped European scholasticism.

summary: Mamluks were slave soldiers, mostly Turkic and later Circassian boys bought from the steppes and trained as elite cavalry. In 1250 the mamluks of Egypt's Ayyubid sultan seized power, founding a state ruled by former slaves. In 1260 their army under Qutuz and Baybars defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in Palestine, halting the Mongol advance, and over the following decades they expelled the last Crusaders, taking Acre in 1291. The Mamluks ruled Egypt, Syria and the holy cities of Arabia, sheltered a figurehead Abbasid caliph in Cairo, and grew rich from the spice trade between India and Europe. Sultans rarely founded lasting dynasties, as rival mamluk factions competed for power. Plague, Portuguese competition in the Indian Ocean and Ottoman firearms ended the sultanate in 1517.
legacy: The Mamluks saved Egypt and Syria from the Mongols, and their mosques, madrasas and tombs make Cairo one of the great treasuries of Islamic architecture.

summary: According to tradition, the Romans expelled their last king in 509 BCE and set up a republic, governed by two consuls elected each year, a Senate of aristocrats and popular assemblies. From its base in central Italy, Rome gradually conquered its neighbours, binding defeated Italian peoples to it as allies who supplied soldiers. Victory over Carthage in the Punic Wars made Rome master of the western Mediterranean, and by 146 BCE it also controlled Greece. Conquest brought great wealth but also inequality and political violence, as generals such as Marius, Sulla, Pompey and Julius Caesar used their loyal armies to seize power. Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE led to more civil wars, which ended when his heir Octavian defeated Mark Antony and became Augustus in 27 BCE.
legacy: The Roman Republic's senate, elected magistrates, checks and balances and idea of citizenship strongly influenced modern republics, including the United States.

summary: After a century of civil war, Octavian, Julius Caesar's heir, became Rome's first emperor as Augustus in 27 BCE, keeping the forms of the Republic while holding real power. The two centuries that followed, the Pax Romana, brought peace and prosperity to an empire that ringed the Mediterranean, linked by roads, a professional army, Roman law and Latin and Greek culture; in 212 almost all free inhabitants became citizens. The 3rd century brought invasions, plague and a rapid turnover of emperors. Diocletian reorganised the empire under several co-rulers, and Constantine embraced Christianity and founded Constantinople. After 395 the empire was permanently divided into eastern and western halves. The West, weakened by Germanic migrations and lost revenue, ended when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476.
legacy: Rome's law, Latin language, roads, cities and adoption of Christianity form the backbone of European civilisation.

summary: The Byzantine Empire is the name historians give to the eastern half of the Roman Empire, which survived for nearly a thousand years after the West fell; its people always called themselves Romans. Ruled from Constantinople by emperors seen as God's representatives on earth, it was Greek-speaking and Orthodox Christian. Justinian I reconquered Italy and North Africa and codified Roman law, but in the 7th century the Arab conquests took Syria, Egypt and Africa. The empire recovered under the Macedonian dynasty, reaching a new height under Basil II, but after defeat by the Seljuks at Manzikert in 1071 it lost most of Anatolia. Crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204. Restored in 1261 but much reduced, it fell to the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II in 1453.
legacy: Byzantium preserved Greek and Roman learning, shaped Orthodox Christianity and the Slavic world, and built masterpieces such as Hagia Sophia.

summary: The Huns were nomadic horse-archers from the Eurasian steppe whose arrival north of the Black Sea around 370 drove the Goths and other peoples into the Roman Empire, setting off the great migrations. By the early 5th century they had settled on the Hungarian plain and built a loose empire over many subject peoples, including Germanic tribes, held together by plunder and Roman tribute payments. Under the brothers Bleda and Attila, and then Attila alone, the Huns ravaged the Balkans, extracted huge sums of gold from Constantinople, and invaded Gaul in 451 and Italy in 452. After Attila's sudden death in 453 his sons quarrelled, subject peoples rebelled and won at the Battle of Nedao in 454, and the empire disintegrated; its last leader, Dengizich, was killed in 469.
legacy: The Huns hastened the collapse of the Western Roman Empire, and Attila became a lasting European byword for a fearsome conqueror.

summary: The Franks were a group of Germanic peoples living along the lower Rhine who served as Roman allies. Clovis I of the Merovingian family united them, defeated the last Roman ruler in Gaul in 486 and the Visigoths in 507, and converted to Catholic Christianity, winning the support of the Gallo-Roman bishops and nobility. Frankish custom divided the kingdom among a king's sons, so it was repeatedly split into sub-kingdoms such as Neustria, Austrasia and Burgundy, then reunited. From the late 7th century the Merovingian kings became figureheads, while real power passed to the mayors of the palace. One of these, Charles Martel, defeated an Arab army near Poitiers in 732, and his son Pepin the Short deposed the last Merovingian king in 751.
legacy: The Merovingian kingdom laid the foundations of France and Germany and made the Franks the leading Catholic power in western Europe.

summary: The Carolingians were the Frankish family who replaced the Merovingian kings in 751. Pepin the Short's son Charlemagne spent most of his reign at war, conquering the Lombard kingdom in Italy, the Saxons, Bavaria and the Avars, until he ruled most of western and central Europe. On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned him emperor of the Romans, reviving the imperial title in the West. Charlemagne governed through counts and travelling royal envoys and sponsored a revival of learning, the Carolingian Renaissance. After his son Louis the Pious died, civil war led to the Treaty of Verdun in 843, which split the empire into West, Middle and East Francia. Briefly reunited under Charles the Fat, it broke apart for good when he was deposed in 887 and died in 888.
legacy: West and East Francia became the cores of France and Germany, and Carolingian scribes preserved much classical Latin literature in a clear script that inspired modern lowercase letters.

summary: In 962 the German king Otto I was crowned emperor by the pope in Rome, renewing Charlemagne's imperial title. The resulting empire, called Holy Roman from the 12th century, joined the German lands with northern Italy and Burgundy, and later Bohemia. Its emperors were elected by leading princes, a system fixed by the Golden Bull of 1356. Emperors clashed with the papacy over control of the Church and with Italian cities over taxes, and real power steadily passed to hundreds of princes, bishops and free cities. From 1438 the Habsburgs held the title almost continuously, and Charles V ruled a vast domain, but the Reformation and the Thirty Years War left the empire a loose federation. Napoleon's victories led Francis II to dissolve it in 1806.
legacy: The empire's layered, federal style of government shaped Germany, Austria and central Europe, though Voltaire quipped it was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.

summary: When the last Carolingian king of West Francia died in 987, the nobles elected Hugh Capet, whose family directly ruled only a small region around Paris. Over the next three centuries the Capetian kings steadily extended royal power over the great dukes and counts, and Philip II Augustus took Normandy and other lands from the English Angevin kings. The Hundred Years War with England, from 1337, nearly broke the kingdom until Joan of Arc helped revive the cause of Charles VII and the English were expelled by 1453. Under the Bourbon dynasty France became Europe's leading power, and Louis XIV ruled as an absolute monarch from Versailles. Debt, inequality and Enlightenment ideas fuelled the Revolution of 1789, and the monarchy was abolished in 1792.
legacy: The French monarchy built one of Europe's first centralised nation-states, and its overthrow launched the age of modern revolutions.

name: Kingdom of England

summary: The Kingdom of England was created when Æthelstan of Wessex, building on his grandfather Alfred the Great's resistance to the Vikings, brought all the English kingdoms under his rule in 927. After conquest by the Danish king Cnut in 1016 and William of Normandy in 1066, England was tied to French lands, and under Henry II it formed the core of the Angevin realm stretching to the Pyrenees. Kings shared power with barons, as in Magna Carta of 1215, and from the 13th century with Parliament. England fought the Hundred Years War against France, lost its French territories and endured the Wars of the Roses. The Tudors broke with Rome and ruled Ireland as a kingdom. In 1707 England united with Scotland to form Great Britain.
legacy: Medieval England developed the common law, Magna Carta and Parliament, institutions later spread worldwide by the British Empire.

name: Kievan Rus'

summary: Kievan Rus grew from settlements of Scandinavian traders and warriors, known as the Rus or Varangians, along the river routes linking the Baltic to the Black Sea and Byzantium. According to the Primary Chronicle, Oleg of Novgorod seized Kyiv in 882 and made it his capital, ruling over East Slavic, Finnic and Baltic peoples. The Rurikid princes collected tribute in furs and slaves and traded with Constantinople, which they also raided. In 988 Vladimir the Great accepted Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium, and his son Yaroslav the Wise issued a law code and built St Sophia's Cathedral. After 1054 the realm fragmented into rival principalities ruled by branches of the dynasty. The Mongol invasion destroyed it, and Kyiv was sacked in 1240.
legacy: Kievan Rus is claimed as the shared cradle of Ukraine, Russia and Belarus, and gave them Orthodox Christianity and the Cyrillic literary tradition.

summary: The Bulgars were a Turkic people from the steppes north of the Black Sea. In 681, after defeating a Byzantine army, their khan Asparukh founded a state south of the Danube, where the Bulgars merged with the Slavic population. Khan Krum defeated and killed a Byzantine emperor in 811, and Boris I adopted Christianity in 864, after which Bulgarian scholars developed the Cyrillic alphabet. Under Simeon I, who took the title tsar, Bulgaria dominated the Balkans and rivalled Byzantium. Basil II conquered it by 1018 after decades of war. A revolt in 1185 founded the Second Bulgarian Empire with its capital at Tarnovo, which flourished under Ivan Asen II but later fragmented. The Ottomans took Tarnovo in 1393 and the last stronghold, Vidin, in 1396.
legacy: Medieval Bulgaria spread Slavonic literacy and the Cyrillic alphabet, now used by some 250 million people.

summary: The Magyars, horse-riding nomads speaking a Finno-Ugric language, crossed the Carpathians around 895 under Grand Prince Árpád and settled the Danube basin, raiding deep into Europe until their defeat at Lechfeld in 955. Árpád's descendant Stephen converted to Latin Christianity and was crowned king in 1000, founding a kingdom organised into counties around royal castles. Hungary joined with Croatia in 1102, survived the devastating Mongol invasion of 1241, and under the Angevin king Louis the Great and the Renaissance ruler Matthias Corvinus became a great power of central Europe. After the Ottomans killed King Louis II at Mohács in 1526 the kingdom was split; the Habsburgs inherited the crown and later reconquered the whole country. Hungary gained equal status within Austria-Hungary in 1867, until the monarchy collapsed in 1918.
legacy: Hungary preserved a distinct Magyar language and identity in the heart of Europe and served for centuries as Christendom's frontier against the Ottomans.

name: Kingdom of Poland

peak.note: Jagiellonian Poland together with Lithuania in personal union; Poland-Lithuania c. 1.1M km² c. 1480 (Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006)

summary: Poland emerged under the Piast dynasty, whose duke Mieszko I accepted Christianity in 966; his son Bolesław the Brave was crowned the first king in 1025. After 1138 the realm split into duchies for nearly two centuries and suffered Mongol raids, until Władysław the Short reunited it and his son Casimir the Great rebuilt it, founding the University of Kraków and welcoming Jewish settlers. In 1386 Queen Jadwiga married Jogaila, Grand Duke of Lithuania, creating a personal union under the Jagiellonian dynasty. The union crushed the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410 and became one of the largest states in Europe. Power gradually shifted to the nobility through the Sejm, and in 1569 the Union of Lublin turned the partnership into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
legacy: Medieval Poland anchored Latin Christianity in east-central Europe and pioneered a parliamentary noble democracy that later produced Europe's first modern written constitution in 1791.

summary: Lithuania was the last pagan state in Europe. Facing the crusading Teutonic Knights, Baltic tribes united under Mindaugas in the 1230s; he was briefly crowned a Christian king in 1253. Gediminas made Vilnius his capital in the early 14th century, and he and his son Algirdas expanded south-east into the lands of the former Kievan Rus, weakened by the Mongols, so that most of the grand duchy's subjects were Orthodox Slavs. In 1386 Grand Duke Jogaila became king of Poland and accepted Catholic baptism for Lithuania. His cousin Vytautas ruled Lithuania at its greatest extent, stretching to the Black Sea. Union with Poland deepened into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1569, which was partitioned by Russia, Prussia and Austria by 1795.
legacy: Lithuania built one of medieval Europe's largest states, and its multi-faith, multilingual tradition shaped modern Lithuania, Belarus and Ukraine.

summary: Venice was founded by people fleeing barbarian invasions to the islands of a lagoon at the head of the Adriatic. Traditionally its first doge, or duke, was elected in 697, and the city gradually broke free from Byzantine rule. Venice grew rich as the middleman between Europe and the eastern Mediterranean, trading spices, silk and slaves. Its merchant aristocracy governed through an elected doge, a Great Council and the powerful Council of Ten, a system that proved remarkably stable. In 1204 Doge Enrico Dandolo diverted the Fourth Crusade to sack Constantinople, giving Venice a chain of colonies including Crete. Venice later conquered a mainland empire in northern Italy, but Ottoman wars and new ocean trade routes eroded its power, and Napoleon ended the republic in 1797.
legacy: Venice was a model of republican government and commerce, and its art, architecture and canals made it one of the world's most celebrated cities.

summary: Moscow was a minor town when Daniel, youngest son of Alexander Nevsky, received it around 1263. Its princes rose by serving the Mongol Golden Horde as tax collectors; Ivan I gained the title of grand prince and persuaded the head of the Russian Church to settle in Moscow. Dmitry Donskoy defeated a Mongol army at Kulikovo in 1380, showing the Horde could be beaten. Ivan III annexed the rich republic of Novgorod in 1478, ended tribute to the Horde after the stand on the Ugra river in 1480, married a Byzantine princess and adopted the double-headed eagle. His son Vasili III completed the gathering of the Russian lands. In 1547 Ivan IV was crowned tsar, turning the grand duchy into the Tsardom of Russia.
legacy: Muscovy was the nucleus of the Russian state, which grew into the largest country in the world.

capital: Córdoba (with the palace-city of Madinat al-Zahra)

peak.note: Most of the Iberian Peninsula plus parts of North Africa under al-Mansur; c. 0.6M km² c. 1000 (Taagepera 1997)

summary: When the Abbasids massacred the Umayyad family in 750, the young prince Abd al-Rahman escaped to Spain and seized Córdoba in 756, founding an independent emirate in al-Andalus. His successors governed a diverse society of Arabs, Berbers, Muslim converts, Christians and Jews, and Córdoba grew into western Europe's largest and most sophisticated city, with its Great Mosque, libraries and paved, lit streets. In 929 Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph, rivalling the Fatimids and Abbasids. Under him and the powerful chamberlain al-Mansur, who raided the Christian north and sacked Santiago de Compostela, the caliphate dominated Iberia. After al-Mansur's sons died, civil war broke out in 1009, and the caliphate was abolished in 1031, splitting into small rival kingdoms called taifas.
legacy: Umayyad Córdoba was a beacon of learning, poetry and architecture whose Great Mosque still stands, and through al-Andalus much classical and Arabic knowledge reached Christian Europe.

capital: Pasargadae, Susa, Persepolis, Ecbatana and Babylon

peak.note: Under Darius I, from Egypt and Thrace to the Indus; c. 5.5M km² c. 500 BCE (Taagepera 1979); c. 5.5M km² c. 500 BCE (Taagepera 1979; Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006)

summary: Cyrus the Great, king of the Persians in south-west Iran, overthrew his Median overlords in 550 BCE and went on to conquer Lydia and Babylon, creating the largest empire the world had yet seen. His son Cambyses added Egypt, and Darius I extended it to the Indus and into Europe. Darius organised the empire into provinces called satrapies, each paying set tribute, linked by the Royal Road and a fast courier service, and introduced standard gold coinage. The Persians generally tolerated local religions and customs, and Cyrus allowed exiled Jews to return to Jerusalem. Attempts to conquer Greece failed at Marathon and Salamis. Weakened by court intrigue and revolts, the empire fell to Alexander the Great, and Darius III was murdered in 330 BCE.
legacy: The Achaemenids created the model of a tolerant, well-organised world empire, and Persepolis remains a symbol of Iranian identity.

summary: The Parthians were an Iranian nomadic people, the Parni, who settled in the province of Parthia south-east of the Caspian Sea. Their leader Arsaces I founded the Arsacid dynasty around 247 BCE and, about 238 BCE, seized Parthia from its rebel Seleucid governor Andragoras. Mithridates I conquered Media and Mesopotamia, and by about 100 BCE Parthia stretched from the Euphrates to Afghanistan, controlling the overland Silk Road between Rome and China. The empire was decentralised, with great noble families and vassal kings holding much power, and its armoured cavalry and horse archers were formidable: at Carrhae in 53 BCE they destroyed a Roman army under Crassus. For nearly three centuries Parthia and Rome fought over Armenia and Mesopotamia. Weakened by Roman invasions and civil wars, the last king, Artabanus IV, was overthrown by the Persian Ardashir in 224.
legacy: Parthia was Rome's great eastern rival for three centuries and kept Silk Road trade flowing; the Parthian shot, a backward arrow fired while retreating, survives as an English expression.

summary: Ardashir, a Persian ruler from Fars in south-west Iran, overthrew the last Parthian king in 224 and founded the Sasanian dynasty, which saw itself as heir to the Achaemenids. The Sasanians built a more centralised state than the Parthians, with Zoroastrianism as an official religion, a powerful priesthood and strong armoured cavalry. Shapur I defeated Gordian III, forced Philip the Arab to buy peace and captured Valerian in 260. For four centuries Persia was the equal of Rome and then Byzantium, fighting over Armenia, Mesopotamia and the Caucasus. Khosrow I reformed taxes and patronised learning. Khosrow II briefly conquered Egypt and the Levant, but a Byzantine counter-attack and civil war exhausted the empire. Arab Muslim armies defeated it at al-Qadisiyya and Nahavand, and the last shah, Yazdegerd III, was killed in 651.
legacy: Sasanian art, court culture and administration deeply influenced the Islamic caliphates, Byzantium and lands as far away as China.

summary: Around 322 BCE Chandragupta Maurya, reportedly guided by the minister Chanakya (Kautilya), overthrew the Nanda kings of Magadha in the Ganges valley. Moving into the vacuum left by Alexander's withdrawal, he conquered the north-west and later won Afghan territory from Seleucus I. His son Bindusara pushed south, and his grandson Ashoka conquered Kalinga in a war so bloody that he turned to Buddhism. Ashoka promoted dhamma, a code of non-violence, tolerance and welfare, carved in edicts on rocks and pillars across the empire, and sent Buddhist missionaries abroad. The Mauryas ruled through a large bureaucracy, spies and a standing army, as described in the Arthashastra. After Ashoka the empire shrank, and in about 185 BCE the general Pushyamitra Shunga killed the last emperor.
legacy: The Mauryas first unified most of the Indian subcontinent, and Ashoka's lion capital and wheel are now India's national emblem and the symbol on its flag.

summary: The Kushans descended from the Yuezhi, nomads driven from western China by the Xiongnu, who settled in Bactria (northern Afghanistan) in the 2nd century BCE. In the 1st century CE Kujula Kadphises united the five Yuezhi clans and crossed the Hindu Kush into northern India. Under Kanishka, the most famous ruler, the empire reached from Central Asia across Gandhara to the Ganges valley. Sitting astride the Silk Road, the Kushans grew rich on trade between Rome, Parthia, India and China, and their gold coins show Greek, Persian, Indian and local gods side by side. Kanishka patronised Buddhism, and Gandhara art blended Greek and Indian styles. From the 3rd century the Sasanians conquered the western lands, and the remaining Kushan principalities faded by the late 4th century.
legacy: The Kushans helped carry Buddhism along the Silk Road to China, and Gandhara art produced some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form.

summary: The Gupta dynasty rose in the Ganges valley, and Chandragupta I took the title great king of kings around 320. His son Samudragupta campaigned across the subcontinent, defeating northern kings and forcing southern rulers to pay tribute, and Chandragupta II added western India. The Guptas ruled the heartland directly and controlled outer regions through vassals. Their era is often called India's classical age: Sanskrit literature flourished with the poet Kalidasa, Aryabhata calculated the Earth's rotation and used a place-value number system, and Hindu temple architecture took shape, while Buddhist monasteries such as Nalanda thrived. From the late 5th century invasions by the Alchon Huns, together with the rise of regional rulers, broke up the empire by about 550.
legacy: The Gupta age set enduring standards in Indian art, literature, mathematics and astronomy, and the decimal numerals it refined reached the world through Arab scholars.

summary: The Cholas were one of the three ancient Tamil ruling families of southern India, mentioned in Ashoka's edicts and in early Tamil Sangam poetry. After centuries in the shadow of the Pallavas and Pandyas, Vijayalaya revived the dynasty around 848 by capturing Thanjavur. Rajaraja I and his son Rajendra I built an empire covering southern India and Sri Lanka, sent an army to the Ganges and launched a naval expedition against Srivijaya in 1025, projecting power across the Bay of Bengal. The Cholas ran an efficient administration with self-governing village assemblies, promoted trade with China and South-east Asia, and built great Shiva temples such as the Brihadeeswarar at Thanjavur. Wars with the Chalukyas and Pandyas weakened them, and the Pandyas ended the dynasty in 1279.
legacy: Chola bronzes, temples and maritime trade spread Tamil culture across South-east Asia, and their great temples remain living places of worship.

summary: After Muhammad of Ghor conquered northern India, his Turkic slave-general Qutb ud-Din Aibak made himself sultan at Delhi in 1206. Five dynasties followed: the Mamluks, Khaljis, Tughluqs, Sayyids and Lodis. The sultans ruled through a Turkic and Afghan military elite granted revenue rights over land, and they repelled repeated Mongol invasions. Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughluq pushed deep into southern India, briefly ruling most of the subcontinent, but rebellions created independent states such as the Bahmani and Vijayanagara kingdoms. Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398 left the sultanate a regional power. Persian became the language of government, and Indo-Islamic architecture such as the Qutb Minar flourished. Babur defeated the last sultan, Ibrahim Lodi, at Panipat in 1526, founding the Mughal Empire.
legacy: The sultanate established Islam as a lasting force in South Asia and fostered the blending of cultures that produced the Urdu language and Indo-Islamic architecture.

summary: Vijayanagara was founded in 1336 by the brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty, in the wake of the Delhi Sultanate's raids into southern India. From their capital on the Tungabhadra river they united the Hindu kingdoms of the south, and for two centuries fought the Bahmani sultanate and its successors for the fertile Raichur Doab. Under Krishnadevaraya the empire covered almost all of India south of the Krishna river. Its capital was one of the largest and richest cities in the world, admired by Persian and Portuguese visitors for its markets, temples and waterworks. Revenue came from land and a busy trade in horses, spices and cotton. In 1565 the allied Deccan sultanates crushed its army at Talikota and sacked the capital, and the empire lingered in decline until 1646.
legacy: The ruins of Hampi are a World Heritage Site, and Vijayanagara patronage helped preserve and develop South Indian music, literature and temple architecture.

summary: After the murder of the fourth caliph Ali, Muawiya, governor of Syria and a member of the Meccan Umayyad clan, became caliph in 661 and made the office hereditary. Ruling from Damascus, the Umayyads continued the Arab conquests on an enormous scale: North Africa, Spain, Transoxiana and Sindh were all taken by the early 8th century, creating one of the largest empires in history. Abd al-Malik made Arabic the language of government, introduced Islamic coinage and built the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. Arab Muslims formed a privileged ruling class, which angered non-Arab converts and supporters of Ali's family. A revolt that began in Khurasan in 747 led to the dynasty's overthrow by the Abbasids in 750, although one prince escaped to found an Umayyad emirate in Spain.
legacy: The Umayyads spread Islam and the Arabic language from the Atlantic to India, laying the foundations of the Islamic world.

summary: The Abbasids, descendants of the Prophet's uncle al-Abbas, overthrew the Umayyads in 750 with support from Persian converts in Khurasan. Their second caliph, al-Mansur, founded Baghdad, which became one of the world's largest cities. The Abbasid state adopted Persian-style court ceremony and a bureaucracy run by viziers, and its early centuries were a golden age: under Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun, scholars at the House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian and Indian works and advanced mathematics, astronomy and medicine. From the 9th century the caliphs relied on Turkish slave soldiers, and provinces broke away under local dynasties. From 945 the Buyids and then the Seljuks held real power in Baghdad. The Mongols under Hulagu sacked Baghdad in 1258 and killed the last caliph, al-Musta'sim.
legacy: Abbasid scholars preserved and built on ancient learning, giving the world algebra, algorithms and much of the science later passed on to Europe.

summary: The Seljuks were a clan of Oghuz Turks from the steppes east of the Aral Sea who converted to Sunni Islam. Led by the brothers Tughril and Chaghri, they defeated the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040 and swept into Iran, and Tughril entered Baghdad in 1055 as protector of the Abbasid caliph, who named him sultan. His nephew Alp Arslan crushed the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071, opening Anatolia to Turkish settlement, and under Malik-Shah and his vizier Nizam al-Mulk the empire stretched from the Mediterranean to Central Asia, with madrasas spreading Sunni learning. After 1092 it fragmented among rival princes, and the eastern branch collapsed after Sanjar's death. A branch in Anatolia, the Sultanate of Rum, flourished at Konya until the Mongols made it a vassal in 1243; it vanished around 1308.
legacy: The Seljuks brought Turkish peoples into the heart of the Middle East and Anatolia, preparing the way for the Ottomans, and their victories over Byzantium helped trigger the Crusades.

summary: The Ilkhanate was the Mongol khanate in Iran, founded by Hulagu, grandson of Genghis Khan, who was sent west by his brother, the Great Khan Möngke. Hulagu destroyed the fortresses of the Assassins and sacked Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate, but his advance into Syria was stopped by the Mamluks in 1260. The Ilkhans ruled Iran, Iraq, the Caucasus and Anatolia, fought the Golden Horde and the Mamluks, and exchanged embassies with the pope and European kings. In 1295 Ghazan converted to Islam and, with his vizier Rashid al-Din, reformed taxation and patronised learning; Rashid al-Din's world history is a landmark. Ilkhanid Tabriz became a hub of trade and art linking China and the west. When Abu Sa'id died without an heir in 1335, the khanate collapsed into rival successor states.
legacy: The Ilkhanate reconnected Iran with China, blending Persian and Chinese art and shaping the later tradition of Persian miniature painting.

summary: Timur, known in Europe as Tamerlane, was a Turkic-Mongol warlord from Transoxiana who made himself master of the western Chagatai lands in 1370. Claiming to restore Genghis Khan's empire, though he ruled through puppet khans and called himself emir, he spent 35 years campaigning: he devastated Iran, crushed the Golden Horde, sacked Delhi in 1398 and defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402. His conquests were brutal, marked by towers of skulls, but he filled Samarkand with captured craftsmen and splendid buildings. After his death in 1405, while marching on China, his son Shah Rukh held the core together from Herat, and his grandson Ulugh Beg built a famous observatory. The empire then splintered among princes and fell to the Uzbeks and Safavids by 1507.
legacy: The Timurid courts at Samarkand and Herat sparked a brilliant flowering of Persian art, architecture and science, and Timur's descendant Babur founded the Mughal Empire.

summary: The Ottomans began as one of many small Turkish principalities in north-west Anatolia, led around 1299 by Osman, from whom the dynasty takes its name. Combining frontier warfare against Byzantium with skilful alliances, his successors expanded into the Balkans, and in 1453 Mehmed II captured Constantinople. Selim I conquered the Mamluk lands of Syria, Egypt and Arabia, and under Suleiman the Magnificent the empire reached Hungary and dominated the eastern Mediterranean and Red Sea. The sultans ruled a multi-ethnic, multi-faith realm through a slave-based elite, including the Janissary infantry, and allowed religious communities to manage their own affairs. From the late 17th century the empire lost territory to Austria and Russia and, despite modernising reforms, was dismantled after defeat in the First World War; the sultanate was abolished in 1922.
legacy: For six centuries the Ottomans linked Europe, Asia and Africa, and their legacy shapes the borders, cuisines and politics of the Balkans and the Middle East today.

summary: The Xiongnu were a confederation of nomadic peoples on the Mongolian steppe. In 209 BCE Modu killed his father Touman and made himself chanyu, or supreme ruler, uniting the tribes into the first great steppe empire. Modu defeated the Donghu and Yuezhi, and in 200 BCE trapped the founder of the Han dynasty at Baideng, forcing China into treaties that sent silk, grain and princesses as brides to the steppe. The Xiongnu state was a hierarchy of tribal leaders under the chanyu's clan, relying on mounted archers and control of trade. From 133 BCE Emperor Wu of Han launched long wars that pushed them back. Civil wars split the confederation: the southern Xiongnu submitted to the Han and settled inside China, while the northern branch was crushed around 89 to 91 CE.
legacy: The Xiongnu set the pattern for later steppe empires and for China's frontier policy, and their pressure spurred early Great Wall building and the opening of the Silk Road.

summary: The Göktürks, or Celestial Turks, were metal-working vassals of the Rouran in the Altai Mountains. In 552 their chief Bumin rebelled, destroyed the Rouran and took the title qaghan, founding the first state to bear the name Turk. Within a generation his brother Istämi and son Muqan had built an empire stretching from Manchuria to the Black Sea, controlling the Silk Road and negotiating with Byzantium, Persia and China. The empire split into eastern and western khaganates around 582, and both fell under Tang Chinese control in the 630s and 650s. In 682 Ilterish revived the eastern khaganate, which reached its height under Bilge Qaghan. Internal strife and an uprising by the Uyghurs, Basmyls and Karluks ended the khaganate in 744.
legacy: The Göktürks gave their name to the Turkic peoples, and the Orkhon inscriptions are the oldest known texts in a Turkic language.

summary: The Tibetan Empire was forged in the early 7th century when Namri Songtsen and his son Songtsen Gampo, kings of the Yarlung valley, united the clans of the Tibetan plateau. Songtsen Gampo founded Lhasa, married Nepalese and Chinese princesses, and is credited with introducing Buddhism and a writing system adapted from Indian scripts. Tibetan armies became a major military power: they fought Tang China for control of the Silk Road oasis cities of the Tarim Basin, and in 763 briefly captured the Tang capital, Chang'an. Under Trisong Detsen Buddhism became the state religion and the first monastery, Samye, was built. A peace treaty with China was carved in stone in 822. After the assassination of King Langdarma around 842, succession disputes broke the empire apart.
legacy: The empire unified Tibet's language and identity and planted the Buddhist tradition that has defined Tibetan civilisation ever since.

summary: In 1206 an assembly of steppe tribes proclaimed Temüjin as Genghis Khan, ruler of all the Mongols. Reorganising his followers into units of tens, hundreds and thousands loyal to him rather than to their clans, he created a disciplined army of mounted archers that conquered northern China, Central Asia and parts of Persia. His sons and grandsons continued the expansion: Ögedei finished off the Jin dynasty, Batu overran Russia and invaded Poland and Hungary, Hulagu took Baghdad, and Kublai conquered the Song. The Mongols ruled through local officials, a postal relay system and religious tolerance, and their peace made Eurasian trade routes safer than ever. After Möngke's death in 1259 the empire split into four khanates, and Mongol rule in China ended in 1368.
legacy: The Mongol Empire connected East and West as never before, spreading goods, technologies and ideas, and also the Black Death, across Eurasia.

summary: The Golden Horde was the north-western part of the Mongol Empire, granted to the descendants of Genghis Khan's eldest son Jochi. After his son Batu's great western campaign of 1236 to 1242 conquered the Volga Bulgars, the Kipchak steppe and the Russian principalities, Batu settled at Sarai on the lower Volga. The khans ruled the steppe directly, while Russian princes kept their thrones as tribute-paying vassals. The Horde grew rich on trade along the Volga and through Black Sea ports, and under Özbeg Khan it adopted Islam. From the 1350s it suffered plague and civil war; Tokhtamysh briefly reunited it, but Timur destroyed Sarai in 1395. It then broke into the khanates of Kazan, Crimea, Astrakhan and others, and the remnant Great Horde was destroyed in 1502.
legacy: Two centuries of Horde overlordship shaped Russian political traditions, and its Turkic Muslim population included the ancestors of the Volga and Crimean Tatars and the Kazakhs.

summary: The Chagatai Khanate was the Central Asian share of the Mongol Empire, given to Genghis Khan's second son Chagatai. It covered Transoxiana, the steppes of Semirechye and the oasis cities of the Tarim Basin. Its khans kept their nomadic way of life longer than the other Mongol branches, and for decades they fought the Yuan and the Ilkhanate, often in alliance with the rebel prince Kaidu. Under Kebek and Tarmashirin the khans began to settle and adopt Islam, which provoked a revolt by the eastern nomads. By the 1340s the khanate had split into a western half in Transoxiana, soon dominated by Timur, and an eastern half known as Moghulistan, where Chagatayid khans ruled until the late 17th century, when the Dzungars took the Tarim Basin.
legacy: The Chagatai Turkic language, named after the khanate, became the classical literary language of Central Asia and the ancestor of modern Uzbek and Uyghur.

summary: The Shang is the earliest Chinese dynasty confirmed by both written records and archaeology. Traditionally founded by Tang around 1600 BCE after overthrowing the Xia, it ruled the middle and lower Yellow River valley. Shang kings governed with the help of relatives and allied lords and moved their capital several times, finally settling at Yin near modern Anyang around 1300 BCE. They practised elaborate ancestor worship, and to ask the spirits about harvests, war and childbirth, diviners cracked oracle bones of turtle shell and ox bone, inscribing the questions in the earliest known Chinese writing. Shang craftsmen cast spectacular bronze vessels, and royal tombs held chariots and human sacrifices. Around 1046 BCE King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king, Di Xin, at the Battle of Muye.
legacy: Shang oracle-bone script is the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters, making Chinese the world's oldest continuously used writing system.

summary: The Zhou, a people from the Wei valley in the west, overthrew the Shang around 1046 BCE. They justified the conquest with the idea of the Mandate of Heaven: Heaven granted the right to rule to a virtuous dynasty and withdrew it from a corrupt one. The early Western Zhou kings ruled through a feudal network, granting lands to relatives and allies who owed loyalty and military service. In 771 BCE nomadic invaders killed King You and the court moved east to Luoyi, beginning the Eastern Zhou. Royal power then faded, and during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods rival states fought for supremacy; yet this was also the age of Confucius, Laozi and the Hundred Schools of Thought. The state of Qin deposed the last Zhou king in 256 BCE.
legacy: The Zhou gave China the Mandate of Heaven and the classic texts and philosophies, Confucianism and Daoism above all, that shaped East Asian civilisation for over two thousand years.

summary: Qin was a frontier state in north-west China that, after the harsh Legalist reforms of the minister Shang Yang in the 4th century BCE, built the most efficient army and administration of the Warring States. Between 230 and 221 BCE its king, Ying Zheng, conquered the six rival states and declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. He abolished feudal lordships in favour of commanderies run by appointed officials; standardised writing, coins, weights, measures and axle widths; built roads and canals; and linked frontier walls against the Xiongnu. He also burned books and was buried with the famous Terracotta Army. His rule relied on heavy taxes, forced labour and brutal punishments, and after his death in 210 BCE revolts toppled the dynasty in 206 BCE.
legacy: The Qin created the first unified Chinese empire and its centralised model of government, and probably gave China its name in many languages.

summary: After the Qin collapsed, Liu Bang, a commoner turned rebel leader, defeated his rivals and founded the Han dynasty in 202 BCE. The Han kept the Qin's centralised state but softened its harsh laws, and made Confucianism the official ideology, recruiting officials partly through examinations in the classics. Emperor Wu fought the Xiongnu, sent Zhang Qian to Central Asia, helping open the Silk Road, and extended Han rule into Korea, Vietnam and the Tarim Basin. Paper, the seismograph and advances in iron-making date from this era. The usurper Wang Mang briefly interrupted the dynasty, but the Eastern Han was restored in 25 CE. Court eunuchs, land-owning clans, floods and the Yellow Turban rebellion of 184 then weakened it, until warlords took over and the last emperor abdicated in 220.
legacy: Han rule defined Chinese identity so strongly that China's majority people still call themselves the Han.

summary: For nearly three centuries after the fall of the Han, China was divided among rival northern and southern dynasties. In 581 Yang Jian, a general of the Northern Zhou, seized the throne and founded the Sui, and in 589 he conquered the southern Chen dynasty, reunifying China. As Emperor Wen he reformed the laws, redistributed land, rebuilt the bureaucracy and began selecting officials by examination. His son Emperor Yang undertook vast projects, above all the Grand Canal linking the Yellow and Yangtze rivers; he also rebuilt the Great Wall and built a new capital at Luoyang, using millions of forced labourers. His three disastrous invasions of the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo drained the treasury and provoked widespread rebellion. Yang was murdered in 618, and his general Li Yuan founded the Tang.
legacy: Though short-lived, the Sui reunified China and built the Grand Canal and the institutions on which the Tang golden age rested.

summary: The Tang dynasty was founded in 618 by Li Yuan and consolidated by his son Taizong, one of China's most admired emperors. Tang armies extended Chinese power deep into Central Asia, and the capital Chang'an, perhaps the largest city in the world with around a million people, welcomed merchants, monks and envoys from Persia, Japan and beyond along the Silk Road. Wu Zetian, the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own name, governed from 690 to 705. Poetry flourished under Li Bai and Du Fu, Buddhism spread widely and woodblock printing appeared. Under Xuanzong the An Lushan rebellion of 755 to 763 devastated the empire, after which regional military governors grew powerful. Peasant revolts, notably Huang Chao's, finished the dynasty in 907.
legacy: The Tang is remembered as a golden age of Chinese culture whose laws, city planning, poetry and Buddhism shaped Japan, Korea and Vietnam.

summary: In 960 the general Zhao Kuangyin seized power and founded the Song, ending half a century of division. Wary of military strongmen, the Song placed civil officials chosen by competitive examinations in charge of government, and the scholar-official class flourished. The economy boomed: rice farming expanded, cities such as Kaifeng and Hangzhou held a million people, and the Song issued the world's first government paper money. Inventions included movable type, the magnetic compass for navigation and gunpowder weapons. Militarily the Song was weaker, paying tribute to the Liao and Western Xia; in 1127 the Jurchen Jin captured Kaifeng and the court fled south, ruling as the Southern Song from Hangzhou. The Mongols under Kublai Khan conquered it, and the last boy emperor died at the naval Battle of Yamen in 1279.
legacy: The Song was one of the most inventive and commercially advanced societies of the pre-modern world, and its Neo-Confucian philosophy dominated East Asia for centuries.

summary: Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis, was proclaimed Great Khan in 1260 and in 1271 declared a Chinese-style dynasty called Yuan. He built a new capital at Dadu, modern Beijing, and completed the conquest of the Southern Song in 1279, uniting all of China under foreign rule for the first time. His invasions of Japan and South-east Asia failed. The Yuan divided society into ranked groups, with Mongols and Central Asians above northern and southern Chinese, and relied on foreigners such as Marco Polo, who claimed to have served at court. Trade flourished, paper money circulated widely and the Grand Canal was extended to Beijing. Later rulers were weak and quarrelsome, and inflation, floods and epidemics fuelled the Red Turban rebellion, which drove the Mongols back to the steppe in 1368.
legacy: The Yuan made Beijing China's capital and joined China, Tibet and Mongolia under one government, a combination later claimed by the Ming and Qing.

summary: Zhu Yuanzhang, a former peasant and Buddhist monk who rose to lead the Red Turban rebels, drove out the Mongols and proclaimed the Ming dynasty in 1368, ruling as the Hongwu Emperor. He rebuilt agriculture and concentrated power in the emperor's hands. The Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing, built the Forbidden City and sent Admiral Zheng He on great treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean as far as East Africa between 1405 and 1433. The Ming rebuilt the Great Wall in the form seen today, and Ming porcelain and silk were prized worldwide, drawing in vast amounts of silver from Japan and the Americas. Later emperors withdrew from government, and factional strife, war in Korea, famine and rebellion weakened the state. Rebels took Beijing in 1644, and the Manchu Qing dynasty, proclaimed by Hong Taiji in 1636, seized the throne.
legacy: The Ming left the Great Wall, the Forbidden City and blue-and-white porcelain, and its silver economy tied China into the first global trade networks.

summary: Goryeo was founded in 918 by Wang Geon, a general from Kaesong, who reunited Korea after the breakup of Unified Silla by 936; the modern name Korea comes from Goryeo. Its kings built a centralised state on the Chinese model with civil service examinations, while powerful aristocratic families dominated the court. Buddhism was the state religion, and Goryeo is famous for its jade-green celadon pottery and for the Tripitaka Koreana, the Buddhist scriptures carved on more than 80,000 woodblocks. The kingdom repelled Khitan invasions, but from 1170 military officers seized power. After decades of resistance it made peace with the Mongols in 1259 and became a vassal of the Yuan, with its kings marrying Yuan princesses. Weakened by pirate raids and factional strife, it was overthrown by General Yi Seong-gye in 1392.
legacy: Goryeo gave Korea its name in the West and pioneered printing with movable metal type; the Jikji, printed in 1377, is the oldest surviving example.

summary: General Yi Seong-gye overthrew Goryeo in 1392 and founded the Joseon dynasty, which ruled Korea for five centuries from its new capital, Hanyang, today's Seoul. Joseon adopted Neo-Confucianism as its guiding philosophy, governing through a scholar-bureaucracy selected by examinations and dominated by the yangban aristocracy, while Buddhism lost its privileges. King Sejong the Great sponsored science and in 1443 created Hangul, a simple phonetic alphabet. Joseon survived devastating Japanese invasions in 1592 to 1598, when Admiral Yi Sun-sin's turtle ships won famous victories, and Manchu invasions in the 1620s and 1630s, after which it became a tributary of the Qing and limited foreign contact, earning the name Hermit Kingdom. Forced open by Japan in 1876, it became the Korean Empire in 1897 and was annexed by Japan in 1910.
legacy: Joseon shaped Korea's language, Confucian social values and national culture, and Hangul remains the Korean alphabet today.

summary: From around 250 CE, the age of great keyhole-shaped burial mounds, the Yamato kings of the Nara basin gradually brought the clans of central and western Japan under their rule. Adopting Buddhism, Chinese writing and Tang-style law codes between the 6th and 8th centuries, they became emperors governing from planned capitals at Nara and, from 794, Heian-kyo, now Kyoto. In the Heian period the Fujiwara family ruled as regents for child emperors, and court culture produced masterpieces such as The Tale of Genji. Provincial warrior clans grew powerful, and after the Genpei War Minamoto no Yoritomo set up a military government, the shogunate, at Kamakura in 1185. The Kamakura regents of the Hojo family repelled Mongol invasions in 1274 and 1281, but strained by the cost, the shogunate fell in 1333.
legacy: This era created Japan's imperial institution, the world's oldest continuous hereditary monarchy, and the samurai culture of the shogunate.

summary: In 802 Jayavarman II declared himself universal monarch in a ceremony on the Kulen hills, freeing the Khmer lands from Javanese overlordship and founding the Angkorian empire in what is now Cambodia. His successors built the city of Angkor near the Tonle Sap lake, supported by a vast system of reservoirs and canals that watered rice fields for perhaps 700,000 people. Khmer kings presented themselves as god-kings linked to Shiva or Vishnu, and later to the Buddha. Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat, the world's largest religious monument, and Jayavarman VII built Angkor Thom and the Bayon and extended the empire across Thailand, Laos and southern Vietnam. From the 13th century wars with the Thai and Cham, strain on the water system and climate shifts weakened Angkor, which Ayutthaya sacked in 1431.
legacy: Angkor Wat is Cambodia's national symbol and one of humanity's greatest architectural achievements.

summary: Srivijaya was a maritime empire centred on Palembang in southern Sumatra, first recorded in the 670s, when the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Yijing studied Sanskrit there. Its rulers grew rich by controlling the Straits of Malacca and Sunda, the sea lanes between China and India, taxing passing ships and suppressing piracy, while drawing on Sumatran gold and forest products. Srivijaya was a federation of port-cities bound to the ruler by oaths, gifts and trade privileges rather than a tightly governed territory. It was a great centre of Mahayana Buddhism, linked with the Sailendra dynasty of Java, which built Borobudur. In 1025 the Chola navy of southern India sacked its ports, beginning a long decline. Rivalry from Javanese states and shifts in Chinese trade weakened it further, and Majapahit absorbed its remnants in the late 14th century.
legacy: Srivijaya helped make Malay the common language of island South-east Asia, the root of today's Indonesian and Malay.

summary: Majapahit was founded in 1293 by Raden Wijaya, a Javanese prince who cleverly used an invading Mongol army sent by Kublai Khan to defeat his rival, then turned on the Mongols and drove them out. From its capital at Trowulan in East Java the kingdom grew rich on rice farming and the spice trade. Under Queen Tribhuwana and her son Hayam Wuruk, the prime minister Gajah Mada vowed to unite the archipelago, and Majapahit claimed tribute from much of modern Indonesia, the Malay Peninsula and beyond, though it ruled directly mainly over Java, Madura and Bali. The court poem Nagarakretagama describes its splendour. After Hayam Wuruk's death, civil war, the rise of Malacca and the spread of Islamic coastal sultanates eroded its power, and it ended in the early 16th century.
legacy: Majapahit is celebrated in Indonesia as a symbol of national unity, and its Hindu-Buddhist culture survives most strongly in Bali.

summary: Pagan grew from a settlement on the middle Irrawaddy, traditionally fortified in 849, into the first kingdom to unite the lands that make up modern Myanmar. King Anawrahta, who came to the throne in 1044, conquered the Mon of lower Burma and adopted Theravada Buddhism, which became the faith of the Burmese people. Under him and successors such as Kyansittha and Narapatisithu, the kingdom prospered from irrigated rice farming, and kings, nobles and commoners competed to earn religious merit by building temples. More than 10,000 temples, pagodas and monasteries rose on the plain of Pagan in about 250 years. So much land was donated tax-free to the Buddhist clergy that royal revenues shrank. Weakened, Pagan was invaded by the Mongols in 1287 and broke apart by 1297.
legacy: The thousands of temples at Bagan are among Asia's great monuments, and Pagan established the Burmese language, script and Theravada Buddhism in Myanmar.

summary: Northern Vietnam was ruled by China for about a thousand years until Ngô Quyền defeated a Southern Han fleet at the Bạch Đằng River in 938. In 968 Đinh Bộ Lĩnh unified the country and founded the kingdom later known as Đại Việt, Great Viet. The Lý dynasty moved the capital to Thăng Long, modern Hanoi, in 1010 and built a Confucian bureaucracy alongside Buddhism. The Trần dynasty repelled three Mongol invasions in the 13th century, and after a brief Ming occupation Lê Lợi restored independence in 1428. The Lê kings pushed steadily south at the expense of Champa. From the 16th century the realm was divided, first by the Mạc usurpation of 1527 and then between rival lords, the Trịnh in the north and Nguyễn in the south, until the Tây Sơn rebellion and the Nguyễn dynasty reunified it, renaming it Vietnam in 1804.
legacy: Đại Việt forged a Vietnamese identity defined by resistance to Chinese domination and by the long march south that created the shape of modern Vietnam.

summary: Ayutthaya was founded in 1351 by King U Thong, who took the title Ramathibodi I, on an island where three rivers meet in Thailand's central plain. The kingdom absorbed the older Thai state of Sukhothai and in 1431 sacked Angkor, inheriting Khmer ideas of divine kingship. Its rulers built a highly organised state, with the sakdina system ranking every subject by land and duty. Ayutthaya became one of Asia's great trading cities, home to Chinese, Persian, Japanese, Portuguese, Dutch and French merchants, and King Narai exchanged embassies with Louis XIV. For centuries it fought Burmese kingdoms; it fell to Burma in 1569, until King Naresuan restored its independence. In 1767 a Burmese army destroyed the city after a long siege, ending the kingdom.
legacy: Ayutthaya shaped Thai monarchy, law and culture, and its ruins are a World Heritage Site; later Thai kingdoms saw themselves as its heirs.

name: Olmec civilisation

peak.note: Gulf Coast heartland in Veracruz and Tabasco, with influence across Mesoamerica (rough estimate)

rulers.name: Olmec rulers (names unknown)
rulers.note: Probably portrayed in the colossal stone heads

summary: The Olmec, who lived in the hot, swampy lowlands of Mexico's Gulf Coast in today's Veracruz and Tabasco, created the first complex society in Mesoamerica. Around 1200 BCE San Lorenzo became a major centre, with earthen platforms and drainage channels, and after about 900 BCE La Venta took its place, with a great earthen pyramid. Olmec rulers, possibly the people portrayed in the famous colossal basalt heads weighing up to about 50 tons, controlled trade in jade, obsidian and other luxury goods across Mesoamerica. The Olmec developed a religion featuring jaguar, maize and rain deities, and probably played the rubber ball game. Their own name is unknown; Olmec, meaning rubber people, is an Aztec word. The heartland declined around 400 BCE, probably because of environmental change.
legacy: Often called the mother culture of Mesoamerica, the Olmec pioneered art styles, religious ideas and the ball game later developed by the Maya and others.

summary: Maya farming villages appeared in southern Mexico and Central America by about 2000 BCE, and by 300 BCE great cities such as El Mirador were building huge pyramids. In the Classic period, from about 250 to 900 CE, dozens of city-states ruled by divine kings flourished in the lowland rainforest, and superpowers such as Tikal and Calakmul fought for dominance through warfare and alliances. The Maya developed the most complete writing system in the Americas, recorded dates in their Long Count calendar, tracked the movements of Venus and used the concept of zero. In the 9th century the southern cities collapsed, probably due to drought, overpopulation and constant war, but northern centres such as Chichén Itzá and Mayapán continued. The Spanish conquered most Maya states in the 16th century, and the last, Nojpetén, in 1697.
legacy: Millions of Maya people still live in the region speaking Mayan languages, and their deciphered inscriptions reveal one of the ancient world's most sophisticated cultures.

name: Teotihuacan

peak.note: A city of perhaps 100,000 people dominating the Valley of Mexico, with influence reaching the Maya region (rough estimate)

rulers.name: Rulers unknown
rulers.note: No royal portraits or names survive; the city may have been governed by councils

summary: Teotihuacan, in the Valley of Mexico north-east of modern Mexico City, grew from about 100 BCE into one of the largest cities in the ancient world, home to perhaps 100,000 people at its height around 450 CE. It was laid out on a grid along a great avenue, later called the Avenue of the Dead, lined with the Pyramid of the Sun, the Pyramid of the Moon and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent. Its people lived in large apartment compounds, some housing migrants from Oaxaca and the Gulf Coast. Teotihuacan controlled the obsidian trade and influenced cities across Mesoamerica; in 378 its envoys intervened in the Maya city of Tikal and installed a new dynasty. Around 550 the city centre was burned, perhaps in an internal revolt, and the population dispersed.
legacy: The Aztecs revered the ruined city, naming it Teotihuacan, the place where the gods were created, and it is now one of Mexico's most visited ancient sites.
